lessons.title: Bash scripting: variables, conditions, loops
lessons.goal:
Write a first useful script: arguments with defaults, `if/elif/else`, `for` and `while` loops, and the special variables.

Why it matters: shell scripts glue together everything on a Linux system: deployments, backups, health checks, cron jobs. A few constructs cover most of them.

setup.note: Each script is saved in a scratch directory and run with `bash` or as an executable.

steps.title: A first script
steps.text: A script is a text file with a **shebang** (`#!/bin/bash`) naming its interpreter. `chmod +x` makes it executable. Variables are set as `name=value` (no spaces around `=`) and read as `$name`. `${1:-world}` means "the first argument, or `world` if none".

code.src:
#!/bin/bash
name=${1:-world}              # first argument, or "world" if missing
count=3

echo "Hello, $name!"

if [ "$name" = "root" ]; then
    echo "careful with that account"
elif [[ $name == a* ]]; then
    echo "your name starts with a"
else
    echo "a regular name"
fi

for i in $(seq 1 $count); do
    echo "for: $i"
done

n=0
while [ $n -lt 2 ]; do
    echo "while: n=$n"
    n=$((n + 1))
done

run.cmd: chmod +x greet.sh; ./greet.sh
run.output:
Hello, world!
a regular name
for: 1
for: 2
for: 3
while: n=0
while: n=1

run.cmd: ./greet.sh alice
run.output:
Hello, alice!
your name starts with a
for: 1
for: 2
for: 3
while: n=0
while: n=1

run.cmd: ./greet.sh root
run.output:
Hello, root!
careful with that account
for: 1
for: 2
for: 3
while: n=0
while: n=1

steps.title: Special variables
steps.text: `$0` script name, `$1`... arguments, `$#` count, `$@` all arguments (quote it: `"$@"`), `$?` exit status of the last command, `$$` PID, `$!` PID of the last background job.

run.cmd: bash -c 'echo "name=$0 first=$1 count=$# all=$@"' prog a b c
run.output: name=prog first=a count=3 all=a b c

run.cmd: ls /nonexistent 2> /dev/null; echo "status of the last command: $?"

steps.title: Tests: [ ] and [[ ]]
steps.text: `[ ... ]` is the classic test command; `[[ ... ]]` is a bash keyword with fewer pitfalls (no word splitting, pattern matching with `==`, `&&`/`||` inside). Numbers use `-eq -ne -lt -gt`, strings use `= !=`, files `-f -d -e -r -w -x -s`.

run.cmd: [ 10 -gt 9 ] && echo 'numeric: 10 > 9'
[[ 10 > 9 ]] && echo 'string compare: 10 > 9' || echo 'string compare: "10" sorts BEFORE "9"'
touch present.txt; [ -f present.txt ] && echo 'file exists'; [ -d /tmp ] && echo 'directory exists'; [[ present.txt == *.txt ]] && echo 'pattern matched'
run.output:
file exists
directory exists
pattern matched

steps.after: The classic trap: inside `[[ ]]` the operators `<` and `>` compare **strings**. Use `-gt`/`-lt` or `(( 10 > 9 ))` for numbers.

steps.title: && and ||
steps.text: `cmd1 && cmd2` runs cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeded; `cmd1 || cmd2` only if it failed. They are the shortest conditionals.

run.cmd: true && echo 'ran because the first succeeded'
false || echo 'ran because the first failed'
mkdir -p newdir && cd newdir && pwd | sed 's#.*/##'; cd ..

steps.title: case
steps.text: `case` matches a value against patterns: good for options and file types.

run.cmd: f=report.pdf; case $f in *.txt) echo text;; *.pdf|*.ps) echo 'document';; *) echo other;; esac

steps.title: Loops over words, files and numbers
steps.text: `for x in LIST` loops over words; a glob gives file names; `seq` or `{1..3}` numbers; `while read` processes lines. Always quote variables that may contain spaces.

run.cmd: for f in *.sh; do echo "script: $f"; done
for i in {1..3}; do echo -n "$i "; done; echo

printf 'one
two words
three
' | while read -r line; do echo "[$line]"; done

steps.title: Arithmetic and reading input
steps.text: `$(( ))` calculates with integers, `(( ))` tests. `read -r VAR` reads a line; `<<<` feeds a string (a here-string).

run.cmd: x=7; echo $((x * 6)); (( x > 5 )) && echo 'x is bigger than 5'
read -r a b <<< 'first second third'; echo "a=$a b=$b"

quiz.q: What is wrong with `name = bob` in bash?
options: Spaces around `=`: bash runs a command called name
Uses $1, or `default` if it is unset or empty
Runs cmd2 only if cmd1 failed

check.scenario: A script must do something only when a file `/etc/app.conf` exists and is not empty. Write the test.
check.answer: `if [ -s /etc/app.conf ]; then ...; fi` (`-s` means exists and size greater than zero). Use `[ -f FILE ] && [ -s FILE ]` if you must also be sure it is a regular file.

lessons.title: Functions, arrays and associative arrays
lessons.goal:
Structure scripts with functions (and know how they return values), and store lists and key/value pairs in arrays.

Why it matters: arrays avoid the quoting bugs of space-separated strings, and functions make scripts readable and testable.

setup.note: Each script is saved in a scratch directory and run with `bash` or as an executable.

steps.title: The script
steps.text: Run it first, then we explain the parts.

code.src:
#!/bin/bash
fruits=(apple banana cherry)
echo "count: ${#fruits[@]}, second: ${fruits[1]}"
fruits+=(date)
for f in "${fruits[@]}"; do echo "- $f"; done

declare -A age=([alice]=30 [bob]=25)
age[carol]=41
for k in "${!age[@]}"; do echo "$k is ${age[$k]}"; done | sort

square() {
    local n=$1                 # local: invisible outside the function
    echo $((n * n))
}
echo "square(7) = $(square 7)"

is_even() { (( $1 % 2 == 0 )); }     # the exit status is the result
if is_even 10; then echo "10 is even"; fi
if ! is_even 7; then echo "7 is odd"; fi

run.cmd: bash lib.sh
run.output:
count: 3, second: banana
- apple
- banana
- cherry
- date
alice is 30
bob is 25
carol is 41
square(7) = 49
10 is even
7 is odd

steps.title: Indexed arrays
steps.text: `arr=(a b c)` creates an array; `${arr[1]}` is one element; `${#arr[@]}` the count; `"${arr[@]}"` all elements **as separate words, even if they contain spaces**; `arr+=(x)` appends; `${arr[@]:1:2}` is a slice.

run.cmd: files=('my notes.txt' 'plan b.md' 'x.sh'); echo "count: ${#files[@]}"; for f in "${files[@]}"; do echo "[$f]"; done
echo "slice: ${files[@]:1:2}"; echo "unquoted splits at spaces:"; for f in ${files[@]}; do echo "[$f]"; done | wc -l
run.output:
slice: plan b.md x.sh
unquoted splits at spaces:
5

steps.after: Quoted `"${files[@]}"` gives 3 words; unquoted it gives 5, breaking names with spaces. This is the main reason to use arrays.

steps.title: Associative arrays
steps.text: `declare -A` creates a key/value map (bash 4+). `${!age[@]}` lists the keys. Order is **not** guaranteed: sort when you need stable output.

run.cmd: declare -A port=([http]=80 [https]=443 [ssh]=22); port[dns]=53; for k in "${!port[@]}"; do echo "$k=${port[$k]}"; done | sort
echo "has ssh: ${port[ssh]:-no}, has ftp: ${port[ftp]:-no}"

steps.title: Functions return text or a status
steps.text: A function **outputs** values (captured with `$(...)`) and **returns** a small status (0 to 255) that `if` tests. Never use `return` for data. Variables set in a function are global unless declared `local`.

run.cmd: f() { x=1; local y=2; echo "inside: $x $y"; }; f; echo "outside: x=$x y=${y:-unset}"
ok() { return 0; }; bad() { return 3; }; ok; echo "ok -> $?"; bad; echo "bad -> $?"

steps.under: A function runs in the **current shell**, not in a new process, which is why it can change your variables and `cd`. Calling it in `$(...)` or a pipeline runs it in a subshell, so its variable changes are lost. Functions are looked up before programs, which is why `type NAME` shows `NAME is a function`.

steps.title: Arguments inside functions
steps.text: Functions have their own `$1`, `$@`, `$#`. Pass all arguments through with `"$@"`.

run.cmd: show() { echo "got $# args: first=$1"; for a in "$@"; do echo "  <$a>"; done; }; show 'a b' c

options: Each element as a separate word, spaces preserved

quiz.q: How do you get a function's data into a variable?
quiz.explain: Output is captured; return is only a status.

options: Limits a variable to the function

quiz.q: Is the key order of an associative array stable?
options: No, sort the keys if you need order

check.scenario: A script loops over `$(ls)` and breaks on files with spaces. Give the robust rewrite.
check.answer: Use a glob, not `ls`: `for f in ./*; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; echo "$f"; done`, or an array: `files=(./*); for f in "${files[@]}"; do ...; done`. For recursive lists use `find ... -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do ...; done`.

lessons.title: Error handling: set -euo pipefail, trap and exit codes
lessons.goal:
Make scripts fail loudly and clean up after themselves: `set -e`, `-u`, `pipefail`, `trap`, and the traps of `set -e`.

Why it matters: by default bash **continues after errors**. A script that deletes `$DIR/*` with an empty `$DIR` is a famous disaster. Strict mode and cleanup traps prevent most of them.

setup.note: Each script is saved in a scratch directory and run with `bash` or as an executable.

steps.title: Default: errors are ignored
steps.text: Without options, a failing command only sets `$?`. The script goes on.

run.cmd: bash -c 'false; echo "still running after a failure"'

steps.title: set -e: stop at the first failure
steps.text: `set -e` exits the script when a command fails (returns non-zero).

run.cmd: bash -c 'set -e; false; echo "never printed"'; echo "exit status: $?"

steps.title: set -u: unset variables are errors
steps.text: `set -u` makes using an undefined variable an error instead of an empty string. It would catch `rm -rf "$DIR/"*` with a mistyped variable name.

run.cmd: bash -c 'set -u; echo "value: $undefined_name"' 2>&1 | sed 's/^bash: line [0-9]*: //'; echo "exit status: ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"

steps.title: pipefail: failures inside pipelines
steps.text: The status of a pipeline is normally that of the **last** command, so `false | true` succeeds. `set -o pipefail` makes the pipeline fail if **any** command in it failed.

run.cmd: bash -c 'false | true; echo "without pipefail: $?"'
bash -c 'set -o pipefail; false | true; echo "with pipefail: $?"'

steps.title: trap: always clean up
steps.text: `trap 'commands' EXIT` runs the commands whenever the script ends, success or failure. Together with `mktemp -d` it guarantees no temporary files are left behind.

code.src:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"; echo "cleaned up"' EXIT

echo "working in a temporary directory"
echo data > "$tmp/file"
cat "$tmp/missing"           # fails: the script stops here
echo "not reached"

run.cmd: bash safe.sh 2>&1 | sed -E 's#/tmp/tmp\.[A-Za-z0-9]+#/tmp/tmp.XXXX#; s/^safe.sh: line [0-9]+: //'; echo "script exit status: ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
run.output:
working in a temporary directory
cat: /tmp/tmp.XXXX/missing: No such file or directory
cleaned up
script exit status: 1

steps.title: The traps of set -e
steps.text: `set -e` is **not** triggered inside `if`, `while` conditions and in the left part of `&&`/`||`. And an arithmetic expression that evaluates to 0 returns status 1: `((i++))` with `i=0` kills the script.

run.cmd: bash -c 'set -e; i=0; ((i++)); echo "reached"'; echo "exit status: $?"
bash -c 'set -e; i=0; i=$((i + 1)); echo "reached with i=$i"'
bash -c 'set -e; if false; then echo no; fi; false || echo "handled: || suppresses -e"; echo "still running"'

steps.under: Because of these exceptions many experts prefer **explicit** checks (`cmd || { echo failed >&2; exit 1; }`) over relying on `set -e` alone. A good template starts with `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, `set -euo pipefail`, `IFS=$'\n\t'`, a `trap` for cleanup, and `main "$@"`. Run `shellcheck` (a static checker) on every script.

options: A pipeline fails if any command in it fails
quiz.explain: Otherwise only the last command's status counts.

options: Whenever the script ends, including after errors
The expression's value is 0 when i=0, giving exit status 1
quiz.explain: Arithmetic commands return 1 for a zero result.

options: Using a variable that was never set

check.scenario: Review this line: `rm -rf "$BUILD_DIR"/*`. What can go wrong and how do you make it safe?
check.answer: If `BUILD_DIR` is unset or empty it becomes `rm -rf /*`. Use `set -u` and the guard `rm -rf "${BUILD_DIR:?BUILD_DIR must be set}"/*`, which aborts with an error when the variable is empty. Also quote it and prefer deleting a known sub-directory (`rm -rf -- "$BUILD_DIR/out"`).

interview.a: -e exits on a failing command, -u errors on unset variables, -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails. See [the lesson](#/lesson/45/strict-mode-errors).
To stop word splitting and globbing: an unquoted value with spaces becomes several words. See [expansion order](#/lesson/1/expansion-order).
[ is the test command (POSIX); [[ ]] is a bash keyword with pattern matching, && and || inside and no word splitting. Inside [[ ]], < and > compare strings.

interview.q: How does a function return a value?
interview.a: It prints it (captured with $(...)); `return` only sets an exit status 0 to 255.

interview.q: How do you clean up temp files reliably?
When does set -e not stop the script?
interview.a: In conditions (`if`, `while`), in `&&`/`||` lists except the last command, and in commands whose status is tested. See [the lesson](#/lesson/45/strict-mode-errors).

glossary.def: The first line (#!/bin/bash) naming the interpreter of a script.
The number a command returns: 0 success, non-zero failure; in $?.
A bash variable holding a list of words (indexed) or key/value pairs (associative).
set -euo pipefail: stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipeline stages.
A bash builtin that runs commands on signals or at exit.
Creates a temporary file or directory with a unique name.

commands.cmd: for f in ./*; do echo "$f"; done

commands.desc: Strict mode at the top of a script.
Abort if VAR is unset or empty.
